lead: An inverter switches a DC source to make an AC output. After this unit you can draw and calculate the output of single-phase and three-phase bridges, choose and compute a modulation method that sets the voltage and places the harmonics, and explain how current source, multilevel and grid-tied inverters work.
about: This unit turns DC into AC. It starts with the single-phase half and full bridges and their square waves, then puts three legs together for the three-phase bridge in 180° and 120° conduction. Voltage control follows: single and multiple pulses, then sinusoidal PWM in its bipolar and unipolar forms, then space vector modulation, and harmonic elimination, which chooses switching angles to remove named harmonics. The last three chapters turn to other inverter types: the current source inverter, the multilevel inverter and the grid-tied inverter with its current control.

chapters.idea: An inverter makes AC from DC by switching the load between the positive and negative rails, so the output is a square wave whose amplitude is set by the DC bus.
chapters.depth: Half-bridge: two switches and two equal capacitors split the bus, so the load sees ±Vdc/2. Full bridge (also called an H-bridge): four switches in two legs, so the load sees ±Vdc. Each device conducts for 180° — square-wave operation. Cover the output waveform, the Fourier series (odd harmonics only, fundamental peak 4Vdc/π, nth harmonic 1/n of that), rms values, R and R-L loads, the anti-parallel freewheeling diodes, and dead time between the two devices of one leg. Some syllabi call the half-bridge a split-supply inverter.

figure.title: Single-phase full bridge
figure.aria: A DC bus feeds two switch legs whose midpoints drive the load, and the load sees a square wave of amplitude Vdc.

chapters.example: A single-phase full bridge runs from Vdc = 300 V and feeds a 20 Ω resistor at 50 Hz in square-wave mode. Find (a) the rms output voltage, (b) the output power, (c) the rms of the fundamental, (d) the rms of the 3rd harmonic. (a) The wave is ±300 V all the time, so rms = 300 V. (b) P = 300²/20 = 4500 W. (c) Fundamental peak = 4×300/π = 382 V, rms = 270 V, giving 270²/20 = 3648 W from the fundamental alone. (d) 382/3 = 127.3 V peak, rms = 90 V.
chapters.trap: Using Vdc as the half-bridge amplitude (it is Vdc/2), and forgetting dead time: if both devices of one leg conduct together, the DC bus is shorted — shoot-through.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for the IGBT, its anti-parallel diode and switching times; Unit 3 for the idea of a switched-mode source.
chapters.leave: The three-phase version to 4.2, modulation to 4.3–4.5, device physics and gate drives to Unit 1.

chapters.idea: Three legs, six switches and 60°-spaced states give a three-phase output; the conduction angle decides how many devices share the current at any instant.
chapters.depth: In 180° mode each device conducts 180° and three devices are on at any instant, one per leg. The line-to-line voltage is a six-step wave with levels +Vdc, 0, −Vdc: rms 0.816 Vdc, fundamental rms 0.78 Vdc. The phase voltage steps between ±Vdc/3 and ±2Vdc/3. In 120° mode each device conducts 120°, only two are on at a time with a 60° gap, so a leg can never short the bus; distortion is higher and the fundamental lower. Cover the switch-state table, the waveform, and the names six-step inverter and square-wave VSI.

figure.aria: Six gate signals over one 360° cycle: each device conducts 180°, and at every instant exactly three devices, one per leg, are on.

chapters.example: A three-phase bridge in 180° mode has Vdc = 400 V and feeds a star load of 10 Ω per phase. Find the rms line-to-line voltage, the rms phase voltage and the power. Line rms = 0.816×400 = 326.6 V. Phase rms = 326.6/√3 = 188.6 V. Power = 3×188.6²/10 = 10.7 kW. The fundamental phase voltage is 0.45×400 = 180 V rms, so most of that power is at 50 Hz.
chapters.trap: Reading 180° mode as 'both devices of a leg on together' — it means each device conducts 180°, and the two devices of a leg stay complementary. Keep phase and line voltages apart.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the bridge and its square wave.
chapters.leave: Voltage control to 4.3–4.5, the switch states as vectors to 4.5, multilevel versions to 4.8.

chapters.idea: Insert zero-voltage notches into the square wave: the fundamental falls in a controlled way while the DC bus stays fixed.
chapters.depth: Square-wave output has a fixed fundamental of 4Vdc/π peak, so the only way to control voltage is to chop. Single-pulse modulation: one notch per half cycle, pulse width 2d, fundamental peak (4Vdc/π) sin d, rms Vdc√(2d/π). Multiple-pulse modulation: p equal pulses per half cycle, rms Vdc√(on-time fraction), and the first strong harmonic moves up to about order 2p−1. Cover the waveforms, the trade-off between p, harmonic content and switching loss, and the names quasi-square wave, notch modulation and uniform PWM.

figure.aria: Two curves against pulse half-width d: the fundamental follows a sine and peaks at 1.27 times Vdc, while the rms rises as the square root of the on-time.

chapters.example: (a) A full bridge with Vdc = 200 V uses single-pulse modulation with d = 30°. Fundamental peak = (4×200/π)×sin 30° = 254.6×0.5 = 127.3 V; rms output = 200×√(2d/π) = 200×√(1/3) = 115.5 V. (b) It is changed to 4 pulses per half cycle, each 10° wide. On-time per half cycle = 40°, so rms = 200×√(40/180) = 94.3 V, and the first strong harmonic now sits near the 7th instead of the 3rd.
chapters.trap: Putting d into sin in degrees without converting to radians, and assuming the fundamental falls linearly with pulse width instead of as sin d.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.1 for the square wave and its 4Vdc/π fundamental.
chapters.leave: Continuously varying pulse width to 4.4, choosing notch angles to kill harmonics to 4.6.

chapters.idea: Compare a sine reference with a triangular carrier: the duty ratio then varies sinusoidally, so the fundamental follows the reference and the harmonics move up to the carrier frequency.
chapters.depth: Reference amplitude Vm at frequency fm; carrier amplitude Vc at frequency fc. Modulation index ma = Vm/Vc, frequency ratio mf = fc/fm. Bipolar: one reference, one carrier, output switches between +Vdc and −Vdc, fundamental peak ma·Vdc, harmonics clustered around mf and its sidebands. Unipolar: two references in anti-phase (or one reference with two carriers), output takes 0, +Vdc, −Vdc, the effective harmonic frequency doubles and the filter shrinks. Cover overmodulation, the linear limit ma ≤ 1, and third-harmonic injection that reaches ma = 1.15 before clipping.

figure.title: Sine-triangle PWM
figure.aria: A sine reference and a triangular carrier enter a comparator; its output drives the gates of the full bridge, which produces the PWM output.

chapters.example: A full bridge with Vdc = 400 V runs sinusoidal PWM at fm = 50 Hz with ma = 0.8 and mf = 21. Fundamental peak = 0.8×400 = 320 V, rms = 226 V. Carrier frequency fc = 21×50 = 1050 Hz, so the first harmonic cluster sits at 1.05 kHz — far from 50 Hz and easy to filter. With unipolar switching the lowest cluster moves to 2.1 kHz.
chapters.trap: Swapping ma and mf, and assuming unipolar and bipolar give the same spectrum — unipolar pushes the first cluster to twice the carrier frequency.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.1 and 4.3 for the bridge and for notches; Unit 1 for switching loss that sets the carrier frequency.
chapters.leave: Vector-based choice of states to 4.5, deleting specific harmonics to 4.6, grid current loops to 4.9.

chapters.idea: Treat the three-phase voltages as one rotating vector and build it each switching period from the two nearest bridge states plus a zero state.
chapters.depth: The three-phase bridge has 8 states: six active vectors of length 2Vdc/3 spaced 60° apart, forming six sectors, and two zero vectors at the origin. A reference vector of length Vm rotates; each period it is averaged from the two adjacent active vectors and a zero vector. Dwell times T1 = ma·Ts·sin(60°−θ), T2 = ma·Ts·sin θ, T0 = Ts − T1 − T2, with ma = √3 Vm/Vdc. Linear limit Vdc/√3, which is 15.5% more than sine-triangle PWM. Cover sector identification, the seven-segment switching order that splits T0 between V0 and V7, and the name SVPWM.

figure.aria: Six active vectors form a hexagon around two zero vectors at the origin, with a reference vector lying between V1 and V2 in the first sector.

chapters.example: Vdc = 600 V, output 50 Hz, switching frequency 6 kHz so Ts = 166.7 μs, required fundamental phase peak Vm = 300 V, and the reference is at θ = 20° inside a sector. ma = √3×300/600 = 0.866. T1 = 0.866×166.7×sin 40° = 92.8 μs. T2 = 0.866×166.7×sin 20° = 49.4 μs. T0 = 166.7 − 92.8 − 49.4 = 24.5 μs, split as 12.2 μs of V0 and 12.2 μs of V7.
chapters.trap: Using Vdc/2 as the length of an active vector (it is 2Vdc/3), and forgetting that the zero time must still be spent as V0 and V7.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for the six switch states, chapter 4.4 for the PWM frame of mind.
chapters.leave: Modulation of many levels to 4.8, grid current loops to 4.9.

chapters.idea: Choose the switching angles so that named low-order harmonics are exactly zero, instead of pushing them to a high frequency.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. With N switching angles per quarter cycle you can set the fundamental and force N−1 chosen harmonics to zero. For a quarter-wave symmetric waveform the n-th harmonic is b_n = (4Vdc/(nπ))·Σ(k=1..N) (−1)^(k−1) cos(n·α_k), where α_k are the switching instants in the first quarter cycle and the output starts at +Vdc. Set b_n = 0 for the harmonics to delete, solve the equations offline, store the angles in a table. Cover triplen cancellation in three-phase lines and the contrast with filtering.

figure.aria: Harmonic amplitude against order for a notch at 30 degrees: the fundamental is largest, the third is zero and the rest fall away with alternating sign.

chapters.example: A full bridge with Vdc = 220 V has one notch per quarter cycle at α1 = 30°. Find the fundamental and the 3rd and 5th harmonics. b1 = (4×220/π)×cos 30° = 280.1×0.866 = 242.6 V peak. b3 = (280.1/3)×cos 90° = 0. b5 = (280.1/5)×cos 150° = 56.0×(−0.866) = −48.5 V peak. One angle set the fundamental; adding a second angle α2 lets you also force b5 to zero.
chapters.trap: Expecting N angles to remove N harmonics — N angles give N equations: one for the wanted fundamental plus N−1 harmonics. Even harmonics are already zero by symmetry.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.3 for notches and the sin d result, chapter 4.4 for the switching waveforms.
chapters.leave: Hardware filters and their design to other units; closed-loop grid control to 4.9.

chapters.idea: Turn the VSI inside out: hold the DC current constant with a big choke and let the bridge steer that current through the load.
chapters.depth: A large series inductor Ld makes the DC link a current source. The bridge sends Id through two lines at a time, so the output current is a quasi-square of amplitude Id and the load voltage is whatever the load needs. Devices must block reverse voltage, so each IGBT gets a series diode, or the bridge uses SCRs with commutation capacitors. For a three-phase CSI with 120° conduction the fundamental line current rms is about 0.78 Id. Cover the dual relationship with the VSI, the danger of an open load, and applications: induction heating, high-power drives, long cables. Some syllabi call it a current-fed inverter.

figure.title: Current source inverter
figure.aria: A DC source feeds a large series choke that fixes the current, and a bridge with reverse-blocking devices steers it into the load.

chapters.example: A three-phase CSI has Id = 50 A and feeds a star load of 2 Ω per phase. Fundamental line current rms = 0.78×50 = 39 A. In star the line current is the phase current, so the fundamental power = 3×39²×2 = 9.1 kW. The current also carries the 5th, 7th and higher harmonics, which add losses in the load.
chapters.trap: Thinking ordinary IGBTs can carry this bridge — they cannot block reverse voltage without a series diode — and expecting the output voltage to be the square wave instead of the current.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.2 and 4.4 for the bridge states and PWM; Unit 1 for reverse blocking of devices.
chapters.leave: Device selection and snubbers to Unit 1, drive applications to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Stack more switches or cells so the output voltage climbs in many small steps instead of two big ones.
chapters.depth: With m levels each step is Vdc/(m−1), so harmonics and dv/dt fall and each device blocks only Vdc/(m−1). Three families: diode-clamped (neutral-point-clamped, NPC), with m−1 capacitors and (m−1)(m−2) clamping diodes per leg; flying capacitor; cascaded H-bridge, where s separate cells per phase give 2s+1 levels. The phase voltage has m levels, the line-to-line voltage has 2m−1. Cover the trade-offs: device count, capacitor voltage balance, isolated DC supplies, and modulation by level-shifted carriers or nearest level.

figure.aria: A tree of the three multilevel families, each with the parts that clamp or stack the voltage and a note on levels.

chapters.example: A three-level NPC inverter has Vdc = 600 V. Each device blocks Vdc/(m−1) = 600/2 = 300 V. The phase voltage takes three values, +300 V, 0 and −300 V, and the line-to-line voltage takes 2m−1 = 5 values, +600, +300, 0, −300 and −600 V. A cascaded inverter with 3 cells of 100 V per phase gives 7 phase levels and a 300 V peak.
chapters.trap: Mixing phase levels (m) with line-to-line levels (2m−1), and assuming every device blocks the whole DC bus.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4.2 for the six-step bridge that becomes one cell, chapter 4.4 for carrier modulation.
chapters.leave: Cell DC sources and battery packs to Unit 6; grid interface of multilevel units to 4.9.

chapters.idea: On the grid the inverter is a current source: a PLL finds the grid angle and a fast loop forces a sine current into the grid.
chapters.depth: A PLL locks to the grid angle. The DC-link or MPPT loop sets the current amplitude. A fast current loop makes the actual current follow a sine in phase with the grid. Controllers: hysteresis band (simple, switching frequency varies), PI in the synchronous dq frame with decoupling (fixed frequency, zero steady-state error), proportional-resonant in the stationary frame. An LCL filter removes switching harmonics and needs damping at its resonance. Cover anti-islanding, unity and non-unity power factor, and how this differs from an off-grid inverter, which sets voltage.

figure.title: Grid-tied inverter control
figure.aria: Power flows from the DC link through the bridge and LCL filter to the grid, while a PLL reads the grid angle and a current controller drives the bridge.

chapters.example: A rooftop solar inverter delivers 5 kW to a 230 V, 50 Hz grid at unity power factor. Grid current rms = 5000/230 = 21.7 A, so the peak reference is 21.7×√2 = 30.7 A. If the grid voltage rises to 240 V the same 5 kW needs only 20.8 A rms, so the current reference must come from the power loop, not a fixed number.
chapters.trap: Commanding a voltage amplitude instead of a current, and ignoring the PLL, so the current lands at the wrong phase and the inverter pushes reactive power.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 4.4 and 4.5 for the modulator, chapter 4.8 for large units; Unit 6 for PV and UPS context.
chapters.leave: MPPT and battery behaviour to Unit 6; grid codes and protection settings to specialised courses.
